titre: CinemaScope Waited Twenty-Seven Years in a French Lens
accroche: Hollywood’s widescreen rests on a lens invented in France in 1926, born of military research, and one that nobody had wanted.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1953, 20th Century Fox releases *The Robe*, a sword-and-sandal epic whose image is nearly twice as wide as that of the films shown until then in the same theaters. The process is called CinemaScope, and Fox presents it as Hollywood’s answer to television. The lens that makes it possible, however, was not designed in Hollywood, nor in the 1950s. It was invented in France in 1926, and it had been sleeping ever since.

## Compressing to widen

During the First World War, the Frenchman Henri Chrétien works on an optical system meant to replace the wide sights of tanks. This research leads him, in 1926, to the Hypergonar. The principle comes down to two steps. When shooting, the lens compresses the image across its width: on the film, a very wide landscape fits into an ordinary frame, with people abnormally stretched in height. At projection, a lens of the same type in front of the projector performs the reverse operation and spreads the image back out, which regains its proportions on a screen twice as wide. The film, the camera and the projector do not change: everything happens in the glass placed in front.

The invention earns Chrétien, in 1931, the Valz Prize of the French Academy of Sciences. The movie business, for its part, takes no interest. For more than twenty years, the Hypergonar remains a laboratory curiosity.

## What it shifts

What changes is not the lens, it is the industry. In the early 1950s, television empties American theaters. In 1952 come Cinerama, which requires three projectors, and the first 3D films, which require glasses. Spyros Skouras, president of Fox, asks his director of research, Earl Sponable, for a less costly system, one that existing theaters can project without changing everything. It is an assistant of Sponable’s, Herbert Bragg, who remembers the Hypergonar.

Chrétien’s patent has expired. Fox meets the inventor in 1952 and buys the lenses he owns, while ordering its own versions from the American company Bausch & Lomb. *The Robe* is shot with the three best Hypergonar lenses available, despite their flaws: up close, the compression effect is lost, and each shot requires two assistants for focusing, one on the ordinary lens, the other on the anamorphic attachment. In 1954, at the 26th Academy Awards ceremony, Chrétien receives an award for his invention.

The history of widescreen is often told as a race for innovation launched by the fear of television. The Hypergonar’s story says almost the opposite: the technology had been ready for twenty-seven years, and it was the threat that was missing. An invention does not become a standard because it works, but because an industry ends up needing it.

repere.texte: Henri Chrétien invents the Hypergonar in 1926 and receives the Valz Prize of the French Academy of Sciences for it in 1931. 20th Century Fox does not take it up until 1952, and the first CinemaScope film, The Robe, comes out in 1953.

carte.punch: Hollywood’s widescreen comes from a French lens of 1926 that nobody had wanted.
carte.idee: In 1926, Henri Chrétien invents the Hypergonar, which compresses the image across its width when shooting and spreads it back out at projection. The movie business ignores it for more than twenty years. When television empties the theaters, Fox buys it in 1952 and makes CinemaScope out of it.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The rest of the story: the Bausch & Lomb lenses, magnetic sound and the adoption of the process by the other studios.

quiz.question: What allowed CinemaScope to be projected in existing theaters without changing everything?
choix: A film stock twice as wide as the usual 35 mm
Three synchronized projectors side by side, like Cinerama
A lens that spreads back out at projection the image compressed during shooting
Glasses handed out to the audience at the entrance
quiz.explication: CinemaScope does not widen the film stock and does not multiply projectors like Cinerama, nor does it require glasses like 3D films. Everything lies in the optics: the image, compressed across its width during shooting, is spread back out by a lens placed in front of an ordinary projector.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Henri Chrétien work on an optical system during the First World War?
choix: To improve the range of artillery binoculars
To correct the distortion of submarine portholes
To replace the wide sights of tanks
To enable aerial reconnaissance at night
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that Chrétien works during the Great War on an optical system meant to replace the wide sights of tanks, research that leads him in 1926 to the Hypergonar.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What flaw affected the three best Hypergonar lenses used to shoot The Robe?
choix: The compression effect was lost in close-up scenes
They could only film in black and white
They distorted the image at the edges of the screen
They required lighting twice as powerful
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that up close, the Hypergonar’s compression effect is lost, which also required two assistants to handle the focusing, one on the ordinary lens, the other on the anamorphic attachment.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What prompts Spyros Skouras to ask his director of research for a new system in 1952?
choix: Chrétien’s patent was about to be bought by a rival studio
Cinerama and 3D films cost too much for theaters to equip
Standard 35 mm film stock was about to be dropped by manufacturers
Actors now refused to work in black and white
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says that Skouras asks for a system less costly than Cinerama, which requires three projectors, and 3D, which requires glasses, so that existing theaters can project without changing everything.
